basis: Both texts are the paper's Abstract, serving the same role: stating the motivating problem (difficulty learning implicit API usage norms vs. writing norms from limited examples), introducing the proposed interactive/visualization support concept that summarizes many examples/patterns from a corpus, and reporting the key user-study finding (N=16 in query, sixteen users in candidate) showing improved outcomes using the tool compared to a baseline. This matches candidate [0]'s ABSTRACT, which plays the identical structural role of summarizing problem, approach, and study results, despite the different domain (API code examples vs. writing norms).

Both are the paper's Introduction sections, playing the identical structural role: motivating the problem (learning implicit conventions/API usage from too few or too many examples), reviewing the gap in existing tools, introducing the novel interactive system (CorpusStudio vs EXAMPLORE) that summarizes many examples with cognitive supports, previewing the user study design, and listing the paper's contributions. Candidate [1] ('INTRODUCTION') mirrors this exact arc: problem of learning APIs from insufficient examples, prior tools' limitations, introduction of EXAMPLORE as a visualization/navigation solution, summary of the lab study with 16 participants, and a final contributions list -- the same rhetorical structure and role as the query's Introduction.

The query is a whole "Background and Related Work" section that situates the paper relative to prior research (here: writing norms and writing support tools), covering multiple subtopics (norms, learning norms, writing tools with generated/retrieved text, writing tools with corpus text, related-work search tools). This plays the same overall role as candidate [2], the whole 'RELATED WORK' section of EXAMPLORE, which similarly surveys and differentiates itself from several categories of prior work (collection-exploration interfaces, API learning research, API mining/visualization). Both are top-level related-work sections synthesizing multiple subsections' worth of content into one holistic contextualization of the paper's contribution. While paper2 also has finer-grained subsections (3,4,5) mirroring the query's own subsections, the query itself is the whole-section object, so the whole-section candidate [2] is the closest structural counterpart.

The query is a Related Work subsection in paper1 establishing why understanding community norms matters and how newcomers learn them (via literature on writer-based/reader-based prose, cognitive apprenticeship, etc.), motivating the paper's approach to supporting learning of implicit norms. This plays the same role as candidate [4] 'Learning APIs with Code Examples', which is a Related Work subsection that surveys prior literature on why learning API usage from examples is hard and motivates EXAMPLORE's approach of visualizing many examples. Both are motivational related-work subsections citing empirical/theoretical studies to justify the paper's core design rationale, even though the domains (writing norms vs. API learning) differ entirely. Other candidates like [2]/[3]/[5] focus specifically on comparing interface designs or mining techniques, which is a different role (differentiating from prior systems) than the motivational 'why this problem matters and how people learn' role played by the query.

The query is a related-work subsection that surveys prior tools/approaches (writing with retrieved/generated text, writing with corpus-based text) and positions the paper's own contribution (surfacing large-scale prior text examples) as building on and differing from this prior work. This plays the same role as paper2's overall RELATED WORK section (index 2), which similarly surveys prior interfaces for exploring collections of complex objects, API learning research, and API usage mining, explicitly contrasting each with EXAMPLORE's contribution. Both are literature-review sections structured around 2-3 named subtopics that culminate in stating how the current system differs from and builds upon each line of prior work. While candidates 3, 4, and 5 are the individual subsections of that related work (which could also match at a finer grain), the query itself is a whole subsection encompassing two sub-numbered topics (2.2.1 and 2.2.2), making it closest in scope and role to the full RELATED WORK section rather than any single subsection; nonetheless I note candidates 3-5 are secondary partial matches at finer granularity.

Both play the "related work on how users currently find/learn from examples, and why it falls short" role within a Related Work section. Candidate [4] ('Learning APIs with Code Examples') reviews prior work on how programmers search for code examples, showing that search results are hard to browse and limited in coverage, motivating EXAMPLORE's approach of visualizing many examples at once. The query subsection similarly reviews existing search/related-work tools (Google Scholar, citation-context tools, recommendation systems) and argues they surface topically similar but not structurally/analogously relevant snippets, motivating the paper's integrated writing-support design. Both sections critique existing example/reference-finding tools as inadequate for the specific need (comprehensive API usage vs. specific writing conventions) and set up the paper's novel contribution. A secondary link exists to candidate [2]/[3] (broader related-work), but [4] is the most specific and structurally parallel match since it centers on 'finding examples for learning/use' shortcomings, exactly mirroring the query's focus on 'finding relevant examples' shortcomings.

The query is a broad "system section" describing CorpusStudio's core concept (retrieving/rendering corpus examples via a code-skeleton-like structure), its design rationale, and features/implementation in one combined section (labeled Section 3). This most closely mirrors candidate [6] "SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON," which is the section introducing EXAMPLORE's core representational concept -- summarizing many examples into one structured, navigable view grounded in theory of what users need to learn (analogous to CorpusStudio's design goals grounded in Variation/Structural Alignment Theory). Both serve as the central "what is our system's core mechanism and why" section of their papers. While EXAMPLORE splits scenario walkthrough (candidate 7) and implementation (candidate 8) into separate sections, the query section bundles motivation, scenario, design rationale, and implementation together, so no single candidate is an exact structural twin; but the skeleton section is the closest in role as it introduces the core artifact/mechanism representation and its rationale, which is the centerpiece of the query. The scenario-walkthrough portion of the query (Alice) also parallels candidate [7], and the implementation portion parallels candidate [8], but the skeleton concept and its motivating theory is the dominant, defining content of the query section overall.

The query is a "Design Goals" subsection that states the high-level motivating goals guiding the design of the paper's tool (Corpus Studio) before describing its architecture/features. The closest role-match in paper2 is the INTRODUCTION section [1], which similarly articulates the motivating problem and the overarching goals/approach that led to EXAMPLORE's design (e.g., "we aim to visualize hundreds of concrete code examples... to reveal their commonalities and variances" and posing the research question that shapes the tool's design). While paper2 does not have a dedicated "Design Goals" subsection, the SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON section [6] also partially reflects design rationale, but it is more about the concrete feature set than abstract design goals. The introduction's articulation of the design aim (helping users understand commonalities/variances, drill down to details) is the closest functional counterpart to the query's statement of design goals.

The query is a walkthrough scenario narrating a persona (Alice) using CorpusStudio step-by-step to accomplish a real task (drafting a paper section), illustrating interface features (browsing clusters, retrieving sentences, filtering) through concrete interaction. Candidate [7] 'SCENARIO: INTERACTING WITH CODE DISTRIBUTIONS' plays the exact same role in paper2: it follows a persona (Victor) through a sequence of interactions with EXAMPLORE (viewing the skeleton, selecting features, filtering examples, drilling into code) to demonstrate the tool's use in practice. Both are narrative usage-scenario sections meant to ground the system's UI features in a realistic task, rather than being an abstract, evaluation, or implementation description.

The query is a subsection describing CorpusStudio's system design/architecture: its theoretical foundations (Variation Theory, Structural Alignment Theory), UI components (text editor, cluster visualization of section titles, sentence retrieval, rendering modes, notes, tooltips), i.e., a detailed "how the system works and what design principles ground it" section. In paper2, the closest structural counterpart is the SYNTHETIC CODE SKELETON section (candidate 6), which similarly describes the core visualization concept's theoretical grounding (drawing on studies of API learning barriers/coordination and use barriers) and enumerates the concrete design features/components (the seven usage features) that make up the system's central artifact. Both are 'whole section describing the core design construct and its features/theoretical basis' rather than architecture/pipeline (candidate 8) or scenario walkthrough (candidate 7) or related work (candidates 2-5). While EXAMPLORE's system architecture (candidate 8) covers implementation pipeline, the query is more about the conceptual/theoretical design and feature set of the interface itself, matching candidate 6's role most closely.

The query is an "Implementation Details" subsection describing the concrete technical stack, infrastructure, and design/algorithmic choices (web framework, vector DB, kNN retrieval, hybrid vs pure vector search decision) used to build the paper's system. This plays the same role as candidate [8] "SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND IMPLEMENTATION," which describes EXAMPLORE's pipeline phases, data storage (MongoDB), and processing/design decisions for implementing the visualization system. Both are implementation-focused sections explaining how the system was built technically, distinct from the introduction, evaluation, or related work sections. The more granular subsections (9,10,11) cover specific pipeline phases (data collection, post-processing, visualization) which are narrower than the query's broader implementation description covering the whole tech stack, so the whole-section candidate [8] is the closest match in role.

The query section describes the data collection and processing pipeline for CorpusStudio (collecting papers, sentence splitting, embedding, clustering) that builds the tool's underlying data pipeline -- a system architecture/implementation description. Candidate [8] 'SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND IMPLEMENTATION' plays the same role in EXAMPLORE's paper: it describes the three-phase pipeline (Data Collection, Post-processing, Visualization) for mining and processing code examples into the tool's database, i.e., how raw source material is turned into the structured data the visualization tool relies on. Both sections are the top-level 'how the system's data pipeline was built' sections of their respective papers, covering collection then processing/transformation steps, even though the domains (research paper corpora vs. code examples) differ. The closest sub-level match within it would be 9/10 (Data Collection/Post-processing) but the query as a whole (level=whole, covering multiple pipeline stages) most centrally corresponds to the whole-section candidate 8.

The query describes a specific data-processing sub-step (sentence splitting via LLM, metadata capture) within a larger 'Data & Processing' section, analogous in role to the 'Data Collection' subsection [9] in paper2, which describes a specific data-mining/processing sub-step (extracting and annotating code examples with metadata like type info) within the larger 'System Architecture and Implementation' section. Both are the first concrete technical subsection detailing how raw source material is parsed/processed and annotated with metadata for later use, rather than being an overview (like [8]) or a later processing stage (like [10] Post-processing, which is about normalization/canonicalization rather than initial parsing/metadata capture).

The query subsection describes a concrete technical process step (embedding sentences with a specific model/parameters to enable retrieval) that sits within a larger 'Data & Processing' section of paper1, analogous in role to paper2's 'Data Collection' subsection (index 9), which describes the concrete technical process (mining/AST traversal/slicing with specific tools) used to prepare the corpus of code examples for later use in the system. Both are implementation-detail subsections describing how raw data is processed/transformed into a form usable by the rest of the pipeline, nested under a broader 'System Architecture and Implementation' / 'Data & Processing' parent section. The closest alternative, 'Post-processing' (index 10), is about normalizing already-extracted segments rather than the initial embedding/preparation step, making 'Data Collection' the better structural analogue for the initial data preparation/embedding step.

paper1_subsection_name: Extracting an Ordered Distribution over Section Titles
basis: The query subsection describes the concrete data-processing pipeline step that extracts and clusters raw text (section titles) into canonicalized, ordered distributions with counts to populate an interactive visualization (CorpusStudio). This plays the same role as EXAMPLORE's 'Post-processing' subsection [10], which describes normalizing/canonicalizing raw mined code segments (chained calls, variable names) into canonical options with counts stored for the interface, sitting within the same 'Data Collection/Post-processing/Visualization' pipeline structure. Both are the middle 'processing/canonicalization' step turning raw mined instances into structured, countable options for a visualization tool, rather than the mining/collection step (candidate 9) or the rendering/interaction step (candidate 11).

Both are the top-level 'User Study' sections describing the overall experimental design, participants, tasks/procedure, and materials used to evaluate the tool (EXAMPLORE vs. CorpusStudio) against a baseline (online search vs. Google Docs) in a within-subjects study. Candidate 12 plays the same overarching role of introducing the study design and methodology as the query, with its subsections (13-15) corresponding to the more granular content (API methods/participants/methodology) that the query bundles together at the whole-section level.

The query is a subsection titled 'Participants' under 'User Study', describing the recruitment and characteristics (background, experience, demographics) of the sixteen participants recruited for a lab study. This matches candidate [14], which is also a subsection titled 'Participants' under 'USER STUDY' in paper2, describing the sixteen participants recruited (their academic level, Java experience, prior API familiarity). Both play the identical role: reporting recruitment source and characteristics of the study's participant pool.

The query is the 'Study Procedure' subsection detailing the concrete step-by-step protocol (tasks, timing, conditions, counterbalancing) used to run the within-subjects user study evaluating CorpusStudio. Candidate [15] 'Methodology' plays the identical role in paper2: it describes the within-subjects study procedure for EXAMPLORE, including counterbalancing of conditions/API methods, the training session, code exploration tasks, and post-survey, i.e., the step-by-step protocol of the study. Both are procedural walkthroughs of how the study session was structured and administered, distinct from participant description (candidate 14) or API/task selection rationale (candidate 13), making [15] the closest role match.

The query is the paper's qualitative-analysis section reporting themes, participant quotes, and insights derived from post-study coding of user study transcripts/free responses. Candidate [18] ('Qualitative Analysis') plays the identical role in EXAMPLORE's paper: it reports themes coded from participants' free responses about the interface's strengths, weaknesses, and potential workflow uses (e.g., filtering feature appreciated, confusion about interface, desired future uses), derived via coding of survey/interview data. Both sections serve as the qualitative-findings companion to a quantitative results section, deriving high-level user insights and behavioral patterns from open-ended study data, even though paper1's tool is a writing aid and paper2's is a code example visualizer -- the sectional role (reporting coded qualitative themes from user study responses) is the same.

The query is a qualitative-results subsection showing how study participants perceived and used a specific feature (section title distributions) while performing a document-drafting task, including concrete usage narratives and reactions. The closest role-match in paper2 is candidate [7], the 'SCENARIO: INTERACTING WITH CODE DISTRIBUTIONS' section, which similarly walks through how a user (Victor) perceives and interacts with the distribution-based feature of EXAMPLORE (the code skeleton with statistical distributions of options) to accomplish a task—illustrating usage patterns, noticing common vs. uncommon options, and drilling down based on the distribution. Both texts serve as concrete, example-driven illustrations of how users engage with a distributional-summary visualization feature within their respective systems. The query also has secondary overlap with candidate [16]/[18] (qualitative survey results), but the query's dominant content—detailed walkthrough of engaging with the distribution feature during a task—most centrally mirrors the role of the scenario section in paper2.

The query is a qualitative-results subsection reporting participants' benefits, usage patterns, and free-form feedback about specific interface features (color coding, filtering, exploring examples) from a user study, organized around user quotes and coded themes (P1, P2, ...). Candidate [18] 'Qualitative Analysis' plays the same role in paper2: it reports coded free-response patterns from the post-survey about EXAMPLORE's features (e.g., color highlighting, filtering, exploring many examples at once), quoting specific participants (P16, P3, P4, P7) about strengths, desired improvements, and future usage scenarios. Both sections serve as the qualitative counterpart to a quantitative results section, synthesizing user feedback on interaction features of an interactive system. While the query's paragraphs also touch on content-related benefits (related work discovery, terminology alignment) that don't have a direct analog, the overall role -- qualitative synthesis of participant feedback on specific interface/support features -- matches candidate 18 most closely among all candidates (e.g., candidate 16 'RESULTS' is the whole section which combines both quantitative and qualitative, but 18 is the qualitative subsection specifically, a better level-matched candidate).

The query is a narrow qualitative-results subsection reporting specific user-study findings about a particular interface feature (bookmarking/notes) drawn from participant free responses/interviews, coded into recurring patterns (P1, P4, P10, etc.). The closest role match in paper2 is candidate [18] 'Qualitative Analysis', which similarly reports coded free-response patterns about specific interface features (e.g., filtering, color-coding, exploring examples) with participant counts and quotes (P16, P4, P3, P7), serving the same function of detailing qualitative feedback on discrete tool features within the results section. Both are sub-parts of a broader qualitative/results discussion drilling into how users engaged with particular features of the system, rather than reporting quantitative accuracy metrics (candidate 17) or the overall study design (candidate 12).

The query is a subsection reporting qualitative user-study findings about a specific interface feature (tooltips) -- what participants liked, disliked, and how they used it, based on coded free responses/interviews. Candidate [18] 'Qualitative Analysis' plays the exact same role in EXAMPLORE's paper: it reports coded post-survey free responses about specific interface features (e.g., filtering, color-coding, summarized display), noting what participants found useful, what they criticized (e.g., confusing colors, extra effort to read), and how it fit their workflows. Both are the qualitative/feature-level companion to a broader quantitative results section, focused on user reactions to particular UI elements rather than overall system evaluation (candidate [16]) or study methodology (candidates [12]-[15]).

paper1_subsection_name: Use of Features, Especially Across Writing Stages
basis: The query is a subsection from the Qualitative Results reporting how participants used a tool's features differently across writing stages (early drafting vs. revision) and what strategies they developed to manage feature complexity. This plays the same role as paper2's Qualitative Analysis subsection [18], which reports coded free-response patterns about which features participants found useful, how they envisioned using the tool in their workflows (e.g., "would use EXAMPLORE to explore unfamiliar APIs," feature usage patterns, complaints about complexity/confusion), and future usage scenarios. Both are qualitative findings sections drawing on user study feedback to characterize usage patterns and feature preferences, distinct from the quantitative results (candidate 17) or the overall Results section (16). No other candidate addresses stage-dependent or feature-preference qualitative findings.

The query is a narrow qualitative-results subsection reporting a specific finding from a user study (anti-plagiarism features' efficacy), part of a paper about a writing-support tool. The closest analog in paper2 is its qualitative analysis of the user study (candidate 18, 'Qualitative Analysis'), which similarly reports specific findings/themes from participants' post-survey/qualitative responses about the tool's features and behaviors (e.g., filtering, color use, confusion), serving the same role of presenting a targeted qualitative finding from the study. No candidate in paper2 addresses plagiarism specifically (different domain), but the role -- a focused qualitative finding subsection within the Results section of a user study -- matches candidate 18 (or its parent whole-section 16) most closely. I pick 18 as it is itself a subsection-level qualitative findings report, matching the query's granularity and role.

The query is a "Quantitative Results" section reporting statistical survey/questionnaire results (Mann-Whitney U tests, Likert ratings, feature usage counts) comparing a tool condition (CorpusStudio) against a baseline, to demonstrate the tool's benefits for writing tasks. Candidate [17] 'Quantitative Analysis' plays the identical role in EXAMPLORE's paper: it reports statistical test results (paired t-tests) comparing EXAMPLORE vs. online search baseline on correctness, vagueness, and survey ratings of helpfulness/confidence. Both are the quantitative-evaluation subsection following a user study, presenting significance tests and descriptive stats about tool vs. baseline performance. The qualitative/free-response findings in the query (e.g., norm-breaking reflections) are secondary and better match candidate [18] Qualitative Analysis, but the primary content here is the quantitative statistical comparisons, aligning with [17].

The query subsection presents quantitative results (statistical tests, participant ratings) comparing the proposed tool (CorpusStudio) against a baseline for a specific study task, drawing on survey/Likert data and correctness/preference statistics. Candidate [17] 'Quantitative Analysis' plays the same role: it reports statistically significant differences (paired t-tests, p-values) comparing EXAMPLORE vs. online search baseline on correctness, confidence, and survey ratings. Both are the quantitative-results subsection of a user study comparing a new interactive visualization tool to a conventional baseline, even though domains differ (writing outlines vs. API code exploration). The qualitative aspects mentioned in the query (e.g., 7.1.4 participant perceptions) are secondary and better match candidate [18], but the primary quantitative-comparison role aligns with [17].

paper1_subsection_name: Task 2: Writing a Section of a Manuscript
basis: The query is a subsection reporting quantitative user-study results (NASA-TLX workload, feature usage counts, survey responses on usefulness) for a specific task in a within-subjects study evaluating an interactive tool (CorpusStudio) against a baseline. Candidate [17] 'Quantitative Analysis' plays the same role in EXAMPLORE's paper: it reports quantitative results (correct-answer counts, statistical significance, post-survey confidence ratings) from the within-subjects user study comparing EXAMPLORE to online search. Both are the 'quantitative results' subsection of their respective user studies, presenting statistics, survey ratings, and feature-related findings. The qualitative/free-response content in candidate [18] is a closer match to a different query subsection, not this one, since this query is explicitly framed around quantitative reactions (TLX scores, usage counts, Likert-style survey figures).

Both sections serve the same role: a post-study "Discussion and Limitations" that reflects on conceptual/empirical insights from the user study, discusses trade-offs (e.g., visual/cognitive complexity vs. expressive power), and explicitly notes system limitations (e.g., EXAMPLORE's limitation regarding stale/low-quality examples parallels CorpusStudio's discussion of dataset scope limitations). Candidate 19 is explicitly the "DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS" whole section, discussing what the study revealed, trade-offs between expressive power and visual complexity, and limitations of the corpus/data quality -- structurally matching the query's role of reflecting on conceptual/empirical insights and limitations. Other candidates like RESULTS (16-18) report study findings without the reflective discussion/limitations framing, and CONCLUSION (20) is a wrap-up rather than a discussion of limitations.

The query is a Discussion subsection reflecting on qualitative findings from a user study about what made retrieved content relevant/useful to users, drawing on post-study observations and participant behaviors to characterize the tool's strengths and interpretive nuances. This mirrors candidate [18], 'Qualitative Analysis' under RESULTS, which reports coded free-response patterns about what participants found useful/valuable in EXAMPLORE and how they interpreted the tool's output—both are analyses of how users perceived and made use of the system's results, grounded in qualitative user study data rather than quantitative metrics. Other candidates like [19] (Discussion and Limitations) also touch on interpretive reflection, but that section is more about trade-offs and future improvements to the system itself, whereas the query and [18] both center on characterizing user interpretation/behavior around retrieved/output content.

paper1_subsection_name: Designing a System with Many Retrieved Examples
basis: The query is a discussion subsection reflecting on the design trade-offs of showing many (N=25) retrieved examples at once—balancing cognitive load against the benefit of seeing variation—and lessons learned for future systems. This most closely corresponds to paper2's DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS section (index 19), which similarly reflects on the trade-off between EXAMPLORE's expressive power (showing many examples/features at once) and visual complexity/cognitive overload, and draws lessons for future design (e.g., progressive disclosure). Both are the paper's discussion of what was learned about presenting large numbers of examples simultaneously, including the cognitive trade-offs and implications for future system design, rather than being a related-work, results, or implementation section.

paper1_subsection_name: Designing Writing Support for and with Community Integration, not AI Integration
paper2_subsection_name: Mining and Visualization of API Usage
basis: The query is a discussion subsection contrasting the paper's design philosophy (surfacing real community examples directly, not AI-generated text) against alternative approaches (AI-based writing assistants), arguing why their non-generative, corpus-grounded approach is preferable. The closest role match in paper2 is the 'Mining and Visualization of API Usage' subsection, which explicitly contrasts EXAMPLORE's approach (instantiating a code skeleton with traceable, concrete examples) against alternative techniques (e.g., Buse et al.'s synthesized human-readable API usage code, GrouMiner's un-parsed synthetic code) that generate/synthesize output rather than preserving traceability to real concrete examples -- paralleling the query's argument that surfacing real examples (vs. AI-generated text) preserves authenticity and community-validated quality. Both passages justify a design choice to ground the system in real, verifiable source material rather than synthesized/generated output. No other candidate makes this specific 'grounded-in-real-examples vs generated/synthesized' argument as its central role; other related-work subsections (interfaces, learning APIs) don't address this generation-vs-retrieval distinction.

The query is a discussion subsection reflecting on how the paper's design choices (embedding metacognitive strategies, sidebars, self-reflection notes) relate to prior work and what this means for the interface design going forward. This plays the same role as paper2's DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS section, which reflects on what the study/design results reveal about the tool's benefits, trade-offs, and interpretation in light of the design goals (e.g., discussing how EXAMPLORE's visual complexity trade-off relates to design decisions, and connecting results back to broader design principles). Both are reflective 'discussion' sections situated after presenting results, interpreting the significance of design choices rather than introducing new mechanisms or reporting raw results. No candidate in paper2 specifically discusses embedding cognitive/metacognitive strategies into UI the way the query does, but the closest role-match is the discussion section that reflects on design implications.

The query is a 'Limitations and Future Work' subsection within a Discussion section, reflecting on generalizability of findings (limited participant background, narrow corpus/task scope) and proposing future research directions. Candidate 19, 'DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS', plays the same structural role in EXAMPLORE's paper: it discusses trade-offs (e.g., expressive power vs. visual complexity), acknowledges scope limitations (e.g., not guarding against stale/low-quality examples), and suggests future directions (progressive disclosure, alternative sorting criteria, additional information scent). Both sections serve as the paper's closing reflective discussion on caveats and next steps, making this the clearest role match despite differing subject matter (writing support vs. API usage visualization).

The query is the Conclusion section of CorpusStudio, summarizing the system's contribution (retrieval-based writing support integrated into drafting, comparison against curated corpora, preserving attribution) and the broader interaction model it exemplifies. This plays the same structural role as candidate [20] CONCLUSION for EXAMPLORE, which likewise recaps the paper's core contribution (synthetic code skeleton visualization for exploring code examples), summarizes evaluation findings, and gestures at future/broader implications. Both are final wrap-up sections restating what the tool contributes and its significance, rather than detailing specific results (as in RESULTS/DISCUSSION) or introducing the problem (INTRODUCTION/ABSTRACT). Hence index 20 is the clearest role match.

Both are the paper's Acknowledgments sections, serving the identical role of crediting funding sources, grants, and contributors/support for the research. Candidate 21 lists grant numbers (AFRL, NSF) and thanks contributors, matching the query's role of disclosing funding and support (NSF grant, DFG, Sloan Fellowship) and disclaimers.
Both are empty placeholder entries with no body paragraphs and no question -- matched via the exact-name fallback for content-empty candidates.
